title: Can a 38-Year-Old Soccer Star Help America Fall in Love with the World Cup?
summary: Imagine you're 6 years old, watching the biggest soccer tournament in the world happen right in your own country. That's what Tim Ream remembers from 1994. Now he's 38, and he might get to play in the World Cup again—this time on home soil! The 2026 FIFA World Cup kicks off June 11 in 16 cities across the U.S., Canada, and Mexico. Ream, a defender for Charlotte FC, is hoping to be picked for the U.S. Men's National Team. The roster is announced tomorrow. "I have no doubt that we can win in a knockout stage game," Ream said. He played every minute for the U.S. in the 2022 World Cup. But the team lost in the Round of 16. This time, the pressure is huge. Many people still say America isn't a real soccer country. Ream wants to change that. He wants to inspire a new generation of fans—kids like you! "The biggest hope and dream would be to say we've inspired our own country of 330-plus million people," he said. Back in 1994, the World Cup in the U.S. helped create Major League Soccer (MLS). Ream hopes 2026 will be an even bigger spark. He's ready to do whatever the team needs—start every game, come off the bench, or be a leader behind the scenes. For Ream, it's not just about winning. It's about making soccer matter in America.
why_it_matters: If more Americans start loving soccer, you could see more soccer fields in your town, more kids playing the sport, and maybe even a chance to watch live World Cup games with your family.

background_read: In 1994, the U.S. hosted the men’s World Cup for the first time, and that event helped create Major League Soccer (MLS)—the country’s professional soccer league.
Tim Ream (a 38‑year‑old defender for Charlotte FC and the U.S. national team) was just six years old then and remembers the excitement.
Today, he’s hoping to make the 2026 roster and inspire a new generation of American fans.
Article_Structure: WHO: Tim Ream, a 38-year-old defender for the U.S. Men’s National Team and Charlotte FC.
WHAT: He hopes to make the 2026 World Cup roster and use the event to inspire Americans to fall in love with soccer, just as the 1994 World Cup did.
WHERE: The 2026 World Cup will take place across 16 cities in the U.S., Canada, and Mexico.
WHY: Many still believe the U.S. is not a real soccer country, and Ream wants to change that by sparking interest in a new generation of fans.

perspectives.description: Soccer fans and young players could benefit from more attention and investment in the sport, just as the 1994 World Cup led to the creation of MLS.
Critics worry that the U.S. team may not perform well under such high expectations, and some people still think soccer will never be as popular as other American sports.
Others see the World Cup simply as a huge global party that will bring tourism and excitement, regardless of whether it changes American sports culture forever.
